Customer Churn Analysis — Clustering Analysis¶

Project: Customer Churn Analysis for Advanced Telecommunications Solutions (ATS)

Notebook role: Data Analyst — Clustering Analysis

Author: Ruyu (Grace) Liu

Purpose of this notebook¶

Per the official role brief, this notebook segments customers using K-Means clustering, based on similarities in tenure and MonthlyCharges. The workflow follows the Stage 2 Clustering Analysis deliverables:

  1. Review and select a clustering algorithm
  2. Determine the optimal number of clusters (Elbow Method)
  3. Train the K-Means model
  4. Interpret the resulting clusters
  5. Visualise and label the clusters
  6. Export cluster assignments for the Business Analyst and (optionally) the Predictive Modeling DA

Data used in this notebook¶

The dataset used here was prepared and handed off by the Data Engineer, as two files:

  • clustering_features_scaled.csv — scaled tenure and MonthlyCharges (the only features K-Means is trained on), plus a row_id key
  • full_encoded_cleaned.csv — the full cleaned and encoded dataset (all features, unscaled), also keyed by row_id

These are treated here as an external input, not something already familiar from earlier work in this notebook. Before using either file for modelling, this notebook independently checks that the data is complete, that tenure and MonthlyCharges behave as expected, and explores the relationship between these two features and Churn — all as a standalone starting point for the clustering analysis, rather than assuming any prior exploration.

A note on scope: Not everything here will belong in the final report — sections are written to be thorough for review purposes, and can be trimmed down by the Business Analyst when compiling the final deliverable.

Validating the received data: Both files should have the same number of rows and share the row_id column, since they're two views of the same underlying cleaned dataset. Rather than assume this is the case, it's confirmed explicitly below — this is standard due diligence whenever a dataset arrives from another part of the pipeline.

The merge itself is also validated with validate="one_to_one" — this makes pandas raise an error immediately if row_id turns out not to be a true 1:1 key between the two files (e.g. due to an unexpected duplicate), rather than silently producing duplicated or misaligned rows further down the notebook.

# validate="one_to_one" raises an error if row_id is not a safe 1:1 join key
_ = cluster_df.merge(full_df, on="row_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one")

3. Exploring tenure and MonthlyCharges Before Modelling¶

Before training a clustering model, it's worth understanding these two features on their own terms — where the values sit on their original scale, and how they relate to Churn — rather than treating them as an opaque pair of numbers to feed into K-Means. The analysis below is done independently here, using the unscaled values available in full_df for interpretability.

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 2 (Epic: Clustering Analysis): Determine optimal number of clusters (Elbow Method + Silhouette Score)

4. Determine the Optimal Number of Clusters¶

Two complementary methods are used here, per the Stage 2 deliverable ("Identified the optimal number of clusters using the elbow method"):

  1. Elbow Method — plots inertia (within-cluster sum of squared distances) against k. As k increases, inertia always decreases, but the rate of improvement drops off sharply after the "true" number of clusters — visually, this looks like an elbow bend in the curve.
  2. Silhouette Score — measures how well-separated clusters are (ranges from -1 to 1; higher is better). Used here as a cross-check on the Elbow Method's suggestion, since the elbow "bend" can sometimes be subjective to read by eye.
In [9]:
X = cluster_df[["tenure_scaled", "MonthlyCharges_scaled"]].values

k_range = range(2, 11)
inertias = []
silhouette_scores = []

for k in k_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X, labels))

results_df = pd.DataFrame({"k": list(k_range), "inertia": inertias, "silhouette_score": silhouette_scores})
results_df

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))

# Elbow plot
axes[0].plot(results_df["k"], results_df["inertia"], marker="o", color="#4C72B0")
axes[0].set_title("Elbow Method — Inertia vs. k")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Number of clusters (k)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Inertia")
axes[0].set_xticks(list(k_range))

# Silhouette plot
axes[1].plot(results_df["k"], results_df["silhouette_score"], marker="o", color="#DD8452")
axes[1].set_title("Silhouette Score vs. k")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Number of clusters (k)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Silhouette Score")
axes[1].set_xticks(list(k_range))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("Optimal_Clusters/elbow_silhouette.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

# Save the numbers behind the plots as supporting evidence for the choice of k
results_df.to_csv("Optimal_Clusters/k_selection_results.csv", index=False)

Finding:

  • The Elbow plot shows a steep drop in inertia from k=2 through k=4, with the rate of improvement flattening out noticeably from around k=4 onward — this is the "elbow."
  • The Silhouette Score peaks at k=4 (≈0.476) — higher than k=2 (≈0.411), k=3 (≈0.446), and k=5 (≈0.430). This is a stronger result than typically expected: both methods agree cleanly on the same value, rather than requiring a judgment call between conflicting signals.

Decision: k=4 is selected. It sits at the elbow bend, and also happens to be the single best-separated clustering option per the Silhouette Score — both methods point to the same answer. It also gives enough granularity to distinguish more than just "high risk vs. low risk" (a 2-cluster split), which matters for how actionable the retention strategy recommendations in the final report can be.

Save the Trained Model¶

The trained K-Means model is saved to disk so it can be reloaded later without retraining. The check below reloads it and confirms it reproduces exactly the same cluster assignments.

To use it on new data, the two input features must first be scaled in the same way as the training data (scaled tenure and MonthlyCharges), then passed to model.predict().

In [12]:
joblib.dump(kmeans_final, "Model/kmeans_model.joblib")

# Verify: the reloaded model must reproduce the same cluster assignments
loaded_model = joblib.load("Model/kmeans_model.joblib")
assert (loaded_model.predict(X) == cluster_df["cluster"].values).all(), "Reloaded model gives different assignments!"

print("Model saved to Model/kmeans_model.joblib and verified.")
print(f"Number of clusters: {loaded_model.n_clusters}")
print("Cluster centres (scaled feature space):")
print(loaded_model.cluster_centers_.round(3))

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 2 (Epic: Clustering Analysis): Interpret the resulting clusters

7. Interpret & Label Clusters¶

This is where full_encoded_cleaned.csv gets joined in via row_id, so each cluster can be profiled using the fields that weren't part of the clustering itself — Contract, InternetService, Dependents, and critically, Churn.

Since categorical features in this file are already encoded as 0/1, the file alone doesn't reveal which raw category each number corresponds to (e.g. whether 0 means "Female" or "Male"). Rather than assume a direction, this is checked directly against the original source dataset (Dataset_ATS_v2.csv) below.

In [15]:
# Cross-check the encoding direction against the original raw dataset.
# Note: this assumes row_id corresponds to the raw file's row order (0-indexed) — reasonable
# here since the raw dataset has no unique ID column, but worth confirming with the Data
# Engineer if the encoded file is ever regenerated with a different row order.
raw_df = pd.read_csv("../Data_Preparation/Dataset_ATS_v2.csv")
raw_df_indexed = raw_df.reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "row_id"})

encoding_check = full_df.merge(
    raw_df_indexed[["row_id", "gender", "Dependents", "InternetService", "Churn"]],
    on="row_id", suffixes=("_encoded", "_raw")
)

for col in ["gender", "Dependents", "InternetService", "Churn"]:
    mapping = encoding_check[[f"{col}_encoded", f"{col}_raw"]].drop_duplicates().sort_values(f"{col}_encoded")
    print(f"{col}:")
    print(mapping.to_string(index=False))
    print()

  • Tenure is strongly associated with churn risk, regardless of spend level: the two low-tenure clusters (0 and 1) both have noticeably higher churn than the two high-tenure clusters (2 and 3).
  • Spend level matters most among low-tenure customers: Cluster 0 (low tenure, high charges) churns at nearly double the rate of Cluster 1 (low tenure, low charges) — 49.2% vs. 24.5%. This suggests new customers on expensive plans are the single highest-risk group in the dataset.
  • Long-tenure customers are comparatively safe either way: Clusters 2 and 3 both show low churn (15.7% and 4.8%) despite one being high-spend and the other low-spend — tenure appears to be the dominant protective factor once a customer has stayed long enough.
  • pct_month_to_month is fairly similar (~54–56%) across all four clusters, suggesting contract type alone doesn't distinguish these segments — the split is really being driven by tenure and spend.

Full Distribution Within Each Cluster¶

The table above only shows the average tenure and MonthlyCharges per cluster. To properly interpret the clusters, it's worth seeing the full spread of values within each one, since two clusters could have similar averages but very different internal spread.

In [19]:
# Visualise the full distribution of tenure and MonthlyCharges within each cluster,
# not just the summary means — shows spread and confirms no residual outliers
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

sns.boxplot(data=profile_df, x="cluster", y="tenure", hue="cluster",
            palette=palette, legend=False, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Tenure Distribution by Cluster")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Cluster")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Tenure (months)")

sns.boxplot(data=profile_df, x="cluster", y="MonthlyCharges", hue="cluster",
            palette=palette, legend=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Monthly Charges Distribution by Cluster")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Cluster")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Monthly Charges ($)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("Cluster_Visualisation/cluster_distributions.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

Finding: None of the four clusters show notable outliers in either feature — the boxplots are clean, with no points beyond the whiskers, and the four clusters show clearly separated tenure ranges with minimal overlap. This supports the interpretation that tenure is the primary axis distinguishing these segments — Clusters 0/1 (low tenure) and Clusters 2/3 (high tenure) form two visually distinct groups.

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 2 (Epic: Clustering Analysis): Cross-validate cluster findings against an independent business rule

Independent Cross-Check: Business-Rule Binning vs. Churn¶

As a sanity check on the clustering result, tenure is independently binned into simple business categories using pd.cut() — completely separate from the KMeans model — to confirm the same churn trend holds without relying on the clustering algorithm at all.

In [20]:
# Independent sanity check: bin tenure into simple business categories,
# and compare the churn rate trend against the KMeans cluster results
profile_df['tenure_bin'] = pd.cut(
    profile_df['tenure'], bins=[-1, 12, 36, 72],
    labels=['New (0-12mo)', 'Established (12-36mo)', 'Loyal (36-72mo)']
)
profile_df.groupby('tenure_bin')['Churn'].mean().round(3)

This simple, model-free binning shows the same monotonic pattern as the KMeans clusters — churn rate drops from ~47% for new customers, to ~26% for established customers, to ~12% for loyal customers. Since this trend holds under a completely independent method, it strengthens confidence that the clustering result reflects a genuine pattern in the data rather than an artifact of the K-Means algorithm.

Assigning Business-Meaningful Labels¶

Based on the profile above, each cluster is given a descriptive label to use throughout the rest of the report:

Cluster Label Description
0 New, High-Spend — Highest Risk Low tenure (approx. 15 months), high charges (approx. \$81), by far the highest churn rate (49.2%)
1 New, Low-Spend — Elevated Risk Low tenure (approx. 10 months), low charges (approx. \$32), moderately elevated churn (24.5%)
2 Loyal, High-Spend — Low Risk Long tenure (approx. 59 months), high charges (approx. \$93), low churn (15.7%)
3 Loyal, Low-Spend — Lowest Risk Long tenure (approx. 54 months), low charges (approx. \$34), lowest churn (4.8%)

The clearest actionable takeaway:

Cluster 0 (new, high-spend customers) is the priority segment for retention efforts — it combines the largest churn risk with the highest revenue per customer, meaning it's both the most urgent and the most valuable segment to act on.

10. Summary¶

What this notebook did:

  • Loaded the data received from the Data Engineer (clustering_features_scaled.csv, full_encoded_cleaned.csv) and independently validated it (row counts, row_id integrity, missing values) before use
  • Explored tenure and MonthlyCharges on their own terms, and found that churned customers concentrate in the low-tenure, higher-charge region — the basis for using these two features to cluster
  • Used the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score to determine the optimal number of clusters (k=4)
  • Trained a K-Means model on the scaled features and saved it to Model/kmeans_model.joblib
  • Visualised the resulting clusters in both scaled and original feature space
  • Joined cluster assignments back to the full feature set (confirming the encoding scheme against the raw source data first) to profile each cluster (tenure, charges, churn rate, contract type, service type, etc.)
  • Assigned business-meaningful labels to each cluster, based on the actual profiling results:
    • Cluster 0 — New, High-Spend, Highest Risk (49.2% churn)
    • Cluster 1 — New, Low-Spend, Elevated Risk (24.5% churn)
    • Cluster 2 — Loyal, High-Spend, Low Risk (15.7% churn)
    • Cluster 3 — Loyal, Low-Spend, Lowest Risk (4.8% churn)
  • Exported cluster assignments for use by the Business Analyst and, optionally, the Predictive Modeling DA

Key finding for the final report: Tenure is the dominant factor separating high- and low-churn customers, but among low-tenure customers, spend level roughly doubles the churn risk (49.2% vs. 24.5%). Cluster 0 — new, high-spend customers — is the clearest priority segment for retention strategy, combining the highest churn risk with the highest revenue per customer.

Note on scope: As flagged at the top of this notebook, some of the exploratory detail here (e.g. the full categorical breakdown in Section 7) is included for thoroughness rather than because it will all go into the final report — the Business Analyst should feel free to pull only the most relevant findings (likely the cluster profile table, the churn rate by cluster chart, and the final visualisation in Section 8).

Next steps:

  • Business Analyst can pull cluster_assignments.csv plus the key visualisations and the four cluster labels above for the final report
  • Predictive Modeling DA can optionally join cluster_assignments.csv (via row_id) onto the ANN training data to test whether cluster membership improves prediction performance
